extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys/practitioners, PTAB parties, patent examiners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and fact-pattern guidance for evaluating written-description support under 35 U.S.C. § 112 and for assessing obviousness (motivation to combine) on post-grant and appellate review. Focus is on how courts and the Board analyze range claims, scope of disclosure, predictability of the art, and what evidence (including expert testimony) suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (Ariad test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement is met when the disclosure relied on for support 'reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.' Ariad Pharms., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co., 598 F.3d 1336, 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2010).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The level of detail required varies depending on the nature and scope of the claims and on the complexity and predictability of the relevant technology. The inquiry is objective and examines the 'four corners' of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art. The inquiry is a question of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-corners objective inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description is determined by an 'objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look only to the specification (and what it conveys to a POSITA) rather than extrinsic labels; evaluate whether the specification shows the inventor 'possessed' the claimed subject matter at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for written description findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description inquiry is a question of fact that is reviewed for substantial evidence on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal a court asks whether a reasonable factfinder could have arrived at the Board's factual determination; the appellate court does not reweigh evidence absent lack of substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range-claim analysis: 'mere comparison of ranges is not enough'
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims recite a narrower numerical range than the specification's disclosed range(s), it is not sufficient simply to compare ranges; the question is whether the claimed narrower range is part of the invention described in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the broader described range pertains to a different invention than the narrower claimed range, the specification does not provide written description support. Precedents illustrating both outcomes include Wertheim (narrower range supported), Blaser (supported), Kolmes (supported), Baird (not supported), and Indivior (not supported).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of endpoints and internal support for subranges
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not literally recite the claimed subrange, but disclosure of the subrange endpoints or embodiments at or near the endpoints supports that the inventor possessed the claimed subrange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of endpoints expressly disclosed (e.g., specification discloses 'about 75% to about 125%' and 'about 85% to about 115%') and lack of inconsistent statements increases the likelihood a POSITA would understand the narrower claimed subrange to be part of the invention. Conversely, absence of endpoints or inconsistent/overbroad statements (e.g., 'any desired level') can weigh against support (see Indivior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of predictability and complexity of the art on required detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of descriptive detail required to satisfy §112 varies with the predictability of the technology: predictable/electro-mechanical arts require less detail than unpredictable arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For predictable arts, a lower level of detail may be sufficient to show possession of claim limitations (e.g., simple dimensional/range limitations); for unpredictable arts, more precise exemplification or explanation is often required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing whether a claimed subrange is a different invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed subrange results in a different invention (different operability, effectiveness, or other distinct property) than the broader disclosed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification shows values outside the claimed subrange produce materially different results (e.g., Baird where values outside the claimed temperature range caused curling or brittleness) and provides no guidance toward the claimed range, that supports lack of written description for the subrange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness review: divisions of responsibility and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate determination of obviousness is reviewed de novo, while the Board's underlying factual findings (e.g., scope and content of the prior art, differences between the prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, motivation to combine, and objective indicia) are reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review asks whether a reasonable factfinder could have arrived at the agency's decision on the factual predicates; legal conclusion of obviousness is reviewed anew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine (Gartside) as a factual issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine prior-art references is a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial evidence is required to support a finding of motivation to combine; relevant evidence includes explicit teachings in the prior art that invite substitution or combination, statements that selection is a matter of design choice, advantages taught by a reference, and credible expert testimony explaining why a skilled artisan would combine references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence that can support motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that can justify a motivation to combine includes prior-art statements inviting design choices or alterations, explicit advantages taught by a reference (e.g., manufacturability, size reduction, ability to achieve different heating profiles), and expert testimony credibly tying the prior-art teachings to the claimed combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding of motivation may rest on a combination of the references' teachings and expert opinions; the Board may credit testimony from either party's experts to support its factual findings. Courts will sustain the Board's conclusion if substantial evidence (including such testimony and the references' teachings) reasonably supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial-evidence inquiry for agency factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal, the court determines whether a reasonable factfinder could accept the evidence presented as adequate to support the Board's factual findings (the substantial-evidence standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves considering the record as a whole (including conflicting expert testimony and teachings in the prior art) and deferring to the Board's credibility determinations unless no reasonable factfinder could reach the same conclusions.
